question: What are the conditions of halal slaughter, and is non-zabihah or kosher meat permissible?
asked: I have been bombarded with halal and haram, zabihah questions. People are confused: why is there ikhtilaf, why do the scholars differ, can we eat zabihah, non-zabihah?
answer:
In a nutshell, there are a number of conditions to make an animal halal, and some of them are unanimously agreed upon.

Of those that are unanimously agreed upon, number one: that the animal itself be halal. If you have a pig, you can never make it halal. The animal must be halal, so cow, chicken: this is halal. Number one.

Number two: the one who slaughters must have the niyyah to slaughter. This is unanimous. If an animal is killed accidentally, it is never going to be halal. There must be the niyyah to slaughter. This is unanimous.

Number three: the religion of the one slaughtering the animal. By unanimous consensus, the slaughter of an atheist or agnostic or Hindu or Buddhist is not allowed. It is the slaughter of whom? The Muslim, and the believing Jew and Christian, Ahl al-Kitab: "Wa ta'amu alladhina utu al-kitaba hillun lakum." And there is tafsil as to who is Ahl al-Kitab, but for now let us just say that the believing Christian and Jew is Ahl al-Kitab. This is by the text of the Qur'an. So Muslim, Christian, Jew: they must be. If you are an agnostic, an atheist, a Hindu, that slaughter is not allowed. Even if they say "in the name of God", it would not be allowed. This is unanimous; there is no ikhtilaf.

So these are, so far, three that are unanimous. Four is pretty much unanimous: one or two, very few scholars, went against this, but pretty much all four madhhabs have this. The fourth condition is that the blood must be cut in the proper manner, so that it gushes out. When you slaughter the animal, the blood must gush out, from the jugular, from any vein in the neck.

And this is based on the hadith that a man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "O Messenger of Allah, sometimes we are in the desert and we don't have our knives. What can we eat? How can we slaughter the animal," like a rabbit or something, "and sometimes we don't have a knife. What can we do?" The Prophet ﷺ said (the hadith is in Bukhari and Muslim): "Anything that causes the blood to gush out..."

In other words, you cannot take an animal and smack, smack, smack: that is maytah, that is haram. You cannot take an animal and electrocute it to death. You cannot take an animal and trap it in a fox type of trap until it starves to death. It would be haram by unanimous consensus of the 'ulama. It's not allowed. The animal must be slaughtered by a Muslim, Christian or Jew, in a manner that causes the blood to gush out, because we want the blood to exit the body as much as possible. So in this case, if you have a rabbit, they would have taken a sharp rock, let's say, and they would have then managed to slaughter it such that the blood is gushing out. And in the hadith, the name of Allah is mentioned. So all of this is unanimous. There is no ikhtilaf.

Where is the ikhtilaf, the big controversy? It is in the fifth and final condition, and that is mentioning the name of Allah as you slaughter the animal. This is the controversy between the madhahib. Three of the madhahib, the Hanbalis, the Malikis and the Hanafis (you can say the Dhahiris as well, but three of the madhahib), are strict on the bismillah. They say that in order for the animal to be halal, you must mention the name of Allah when you slaughter.

And the evidence is from the Qur'an and Sunnah. Allah says in the Qur'an: eat of that over which Allah's name has been mentioned. And Allah says in the Qur'an: do not eat of that over which Allah's name has not been mentioned. And Allah says in the Qur'an, regarding the animals, the falcons and the hunting animals: eat what they have caught for you, and mention the name of Allah when you send them out. So there are so many ayat that mention mentioning the name of Allah.

And the hadith I just quoted to you right now: when the man says, "I don't have a knife," what did the Prophet ﷺ say? "All that causes the blood to gush out," and what was the second condition? "And you mention the name of Allah over it."

And Ibn Taymiyyah has a treatise on this, an entire treatise on the necessity, the wujub, of mentioning the name of Allah over the animal. And he says the evidences for saying that the tasmiyah, the bismillah, is obligatory are more numerous than those for the obligation of reciting al-Fatihah in the salah.

And he says the most explicit is the hadith in Sahih Bukhari that a man said, "O Messenger of Allah, sometimes I send my hunting animal to catch the prey. By the time I get to the prey, I find other animals as well, and I don't know which one killed the prey: my hunting animal or the wild animals." Do you understand the scenario? Guys, do you understand the scenario? Right: I get to the deer, I get to whatever rabbit I'm hunting, and there's a whole bunch of stuff. My animal is there, the trained animal, and the untrained animals, the wild animals, are there, and I don't know which one killed it.

Our Prophet ﷺ said (this hadith is in Bukhari and Muslim, and Ibn Taymiyyah says this is the most explicit hadith that tasmiyah is wajib): "Do not eat of that meat, because you said bismillah over your animal and you did not say bismillah over the other animal." This hadith is very explicit.

Now, the Shafi'i madhhab is the exception. They have their evidences, but in a nutshell they say all of these evidences merely indicate that it is sunnah and not wajib. Jayyid, that's their position. The Shafi'i madhhab says that saying bismillah is recommended; it is not wajib. Hence, if a Christian or Jew, with the niyyah to slaughter, slaughters the animal and causes the blood to gush out, even if they don't say bismillah, the Shafi'i madhhab says what? It's okay. And the Hanafi and Hanbali and Maliki say it's not okay, not good.

So what do we do in the end? And by the way, there are other issues that are raised as well, and they complicate it. Of them: in the land that we live in, how do we know if the slaughterer is Christian or Jew or atheist? That's another question mark. And another question that is raised is the issue of stunning.

Now, to be very precise, stunning the animal itself is makruh. If the animal dies as a result of the stunning, the animal is haram. But if the animal is alive after the stunning and the slaughter occurs, then technically the animal is halal. But, and this is the big but: what percentage of animals die between the stunning and the slaughter? Scientific surveys differ greatly. Some say 2–3%, and I have read some that say 20–30%. If it's 2–3%, we can ignore it. If it's 20–30%, we cannot ignore it. So there are uncertainties added that, even according to the Shafi'i madhhab, should make them very cautious, because we have all of these issues.

On top of this, to make matters even worse, in the last five or six years the modern abattoirs, the modern slaughterhouses, have pioneered a new technique to cut the animal that minimizes the blood spurting out. They don't care about the blood; they care about the dirt and the filth and the dust. What they have done is they cut horizontally and not vertically, and that minimizes the gushing of the blood. So this is yet another big question mark.

In my humble opinion, and I respect all of the madhahib, the evidences for the tasmiyah are very explicit. As Ibn Taymiyyah said, this hadith: "Don't eat." He made it haram. "Don't eat. You said bismillah over your animal; you did not say bismillah over the other animal." This is a case of 50-50: we don't know which dog or which falcon killed the animal. How about the case of 100%, where you know there was no bismillah given? So in my humble opinion, I am a Hanbali or a Hanafi in this madhhab, or a Maliki, and so I am a strict zabihah person.

But at the same time, my dear brothers and sisters, the Shafi'i madhhab is a legitimate madhhab. So if you meet a fellow Shafi'i, he's not an evil Muslim. You can pray behind him; your namaz is valid, don't worry. You may visit him in his house and return his salam, no problem. I mean, don't make Islam difficult. This is a legitimate madhhab. We respect the madhhab, and we respectfully disagree.

Now, some other points before we conclude. The issue of GMOs, genetically modified and whatnot: a lot of people ask. Generally speaking, our fiqh councils have said that by and large this does not make the meat haram.

The issue of mistreating the animal, the unethical treatment of animals: the animal is not fed properly, or the animal is put in cages, or the animal doesn't have green pasture, or whatnot. All of this, the abuse of animals (and there are many videos that we have seen of cruel farmers beating animals and throwing the chickens and whatnot), is just absolutely haram, and very bad practice. So there has been a movement to say this meat is haram.

And technically speaking, we say the farmers that mistreat and abuse the animals are sinful in the eyes of Allah, and they will be punished if Allah does not forgive them. They have to repent for that. But the farmer mistreating the animal does not make the animal haram for us if it is slaughtered properly.

Now, whether we choose to boycott an unethical farmer or not, that's a totally separate issue, and I'm not advocating either way; I'm being technical. If a farmer is mean to the chickens but he slaughters the chicken properly, that chicken is halal for us. Now, should we buy from the farmer or not? That is an ethical issue. Fiqh says the animal is halal. Ethics might say: why should we support that farmer? Let's support the better farmer. So let's not conflate the two. Technically the meat is halal, but whether you want to find ethically sourced meat or whatnot, that is up to you.

And the other issue that comes up: you have to be practical. Those types of farms are triple the price of the regular ones. We cannot make something wajib upon the ummah that is unreasonable for them. But me personally, as a human being, in my own capacity, I try to find ethical and humane farms. But it's not haram to go to those other ones.

The other issue that comes up is: is kosher halal or not? I have written an academic paper, which is published, and you can find it online as well. It is called "Is Kosher Halal?" by Yasir Qadhi. It's an academic paper that was presented at an academic conference, and **I concluded that kosher meat is halal.** In fact, kosher meat is exactly the meat that Allah mentions in the Qur'an: the ta'am of the Ahl al-Kitab is halal for you. I concluded in my paper that this is a reference to kosher, not to McDonald's.

Because, and here's the point: when the Ahl al-Kitab follow their Shari'ah, the meat is halal for us. When they have abandoned their Shari'ah and they don't care about what their own books say... And I proved in that paper that once upon a time even Christians slaughtered properly. In medieval times, Christians mentioned the name of God; in medieval times, Christians slaughtered properly. Then they went far away from their religion and they left their own Shari'ah. If Christians have abandoned their own Shari'ah, that meat is not halal for us.

But if you find a Christian who's your friend, he's a farmer, he's a hunter, and he says, "I want to gift you some meat," and he's a believing Christian, you say, "Can you say 'in the name of God'?" And he says it: the meat is halal.

Because why is the meat of Ahl al-Kitab halal, and the meat of the Hindu not halal? When the Christian says "in the name of God", he means the God of Abraham. He means the God of Abraham. When the Jew says "in the name of Yahweh"... in the name of God; he doesn't say Yahweh, take that back, it's the tetragrammaton. He says the name of God or whatever; he mentions the Shema of Israel, he mentions the blessing. When the Jewish person says that, who is their God? "Wa ilahuna wa ilahukum wahid." This is in the Qur'an: your God and our God is the same. This is in the Qur'an. The God of the Ahl al-Kitab and the God of Islam is the same. So when the Jew says, "Blessings, O God, before I slaughter this animal," that is the tasmiyah right there. Now, when the Hindu says "in the name of my gods", is that ours? No, it's not.

That is why the meat of Ahl al-Kitab is halal: if they follow their Shari'ah and they mention the name of God, it becomes halal. But if they bang the animal to death, is it halal? If they eat pork, is it halal? If they don't mention the name of Allah, is it halal? No. That is my opinion, and that's the opinion of the three madhhabs. They have to follow their Shari'ah; then it is halal. If they don't follow their Shari'ah, it is not halal.

In any case, to conclude: respect the Shafi'i madhhab if you don't follow it. If you follow the Shafi'i madhhab, no problem. That's why, by the way... Why has this taken on a cultural connotation, our Arab brothers, our Desi brothers? Technically it should not be true, because it's not "Arab brothers"; it's the Shafi'is of the Arabs. Technically, the Malikis of the Arabs and the Hanbalis of the Arabs should not be following this fatwa. Unfortunately many of them do, but technically they should not.

The Hanbali school, and they are my teachers, Shaykh Ibn Baz and Ibn 'Uthaymin and Salih al-Fawzan and all of these Hanbali 'ulama: they were ultra strict about this issue. Go read their fatawa. They would not allow meat to be eaten that did not have the name of Allah mentioned over it. They were very strict. Unfortunately, many of the people who claim to follow that group want to follow the fatwas of the Shafi'i scholars. They pick and choose, because it's tastier that way. And I don't know why the North African brothers... but in reality the Maliki madhhab, generally speaking, does not. I know there's a dissenting view, but the mainstream of the Hanbali and Maliki does not allow for it. It's only the Shafi'i school.

And you know what? Whoever follows the Shafi'i madhhab, alhamdulillah, that's your madhhab. No big deal. Don't make Islam difficult. In some areas one madhhab is strict and another is lax; in other areas the strict madhhab is lax and the lax madhhab is strict. So if you're following a madhhab, no big deal. Remain with your madhhab. If you ask me, then it seems, looking at the evidences, that **mentioning the name of Allah is a necessary requirement from the Qur'an and from the Sunnah.**

I forgot one hadith, sorry. One hadith and we're done. A lot of people mention this hadith; it's in my notes, I forgot to mention it. That hadith is: "Why don't you mention the name of Allah, then eat?" You know that hadith? Have you heard it? "You mention the name of Allah, then eat." This hadith is actually misunderstood. All you need to do is look at the context of the hadith. The hadith is in Sahih Bukhari; it's an authentic hadith. The Sahabah said, "Ya Rasulallah, there is a group of new Muslims," hadithu 'ahdin bil-Islam, they just converted, "and we do not know: are they saying bismillah or not?" Notice this hadith is in a very specific context. It's in Sahih Bukhari: wa la nadri, are they saying bismillah or not?

Now, when the Muslim slaughters, what is the default? Does he say it or not? He says it. So if a Muslim slaughters, we don't need to have security cameras. If it's a pious Muslim, if it's a Muslim we know coming to the masjid, we don't have to spy. So the Prophet ﷺ said, about the Muslim cutting the animal: if you feel doubtful, in this case you say bismillah and you eat. The hadith is not about when we know for a fact they don't have bismillah. That would be a separate thing, and that goes back to the hadith of the two animals: if it's 50-50, we take the animal to be haram.

So this hadith is misapplied. It's only applied when a Muslim is slaughtering and you're unsure: do they know the rules of slaughter or not? Are they a brand new Muslim or not? In this case you say bismillah and you leave their affair to Allah. But when you know that they haven't said bismillah... And the slaughterhouses of this country do not say bismillah unless they are halal or kosher. Unless they are halal or kosher: they are the ones that say bismillah, and it is not a problem to buy from there.
